questions.problem: A syrup mixing tank at a bottling plant can hold up to $220\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $120\,\text{gal}$ of syrup solution with $24\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved sugar. A more concentrated sugar solution with concentration $0.7\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $8\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of sugar in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the tank minus the rate at which sugar leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $0.7\,\text{lb/gal}$ of sugar enters the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.7\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.7\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =8.4\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the tank.

To find the rate at which sugar leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $120\,\text{gal}$ of liquid; solution enters at $12\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $8\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=120+12t-8t=4(30+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $8\,\text{gal/min},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(8\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(8\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{8Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{30+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =8.4-\frac{2Q}{30+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q=8.4.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(30+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|30+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(30+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(30+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q) & =(30+t)^{2}\cdot 8.4 \\ (30+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(30+t)Q & =8.4(30+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2}) & =8.4(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 8.4(30+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(30+t)^{2} & =8.4\cdot \frac{1}{3}(30+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =2.8(30+t)+\frac{C}{(30+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $24\,\text{lb}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=24,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =24 \\ 2.8(30+0)+\frac{C}{(30+0)^{2}} & =24 \\ 84+\frac{C}{(30)^{2}} & =24 \\ \frac{C}{(30)^{2}} & =-60 \\ C & =-60(30)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =2.8(30+t)-\frac{60(30)^{2}}{(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =2.8(30+t)-60{(\frac{30}{30+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $220\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=220$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =220 \\ 120+12{t}_{o}-8{t}_{o} & =220 \\ 120+4{t}_{o} & =220 \\ 4{t}_{o} & =100 \\ {t}_{o} & =25\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of sugar in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(25) & =2.8(30+25)-60{(\frac{30}{30+25})}^{2} \\  & =154-60{(\frac{30}{55})}^{2} \\  & ≈136.1\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A dye mixing tank at a textile factory can hold up to $180\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $100\,\text{gal}$ of solution with $20\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved dye. A more concentrated dye solution with concentration $0.6\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of dye in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which dye enters the tank minus the rate at which dye leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which dye enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $0.6\,\text{lb/gal}$ of dye enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *dye* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.6\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.6\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =9\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which dye exits the tank.

To find the rate at which dye leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $100\,\text{gal}$ of liquid; solution enters at $15\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $10\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=100+15t-10t=5(20+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of dye in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{5(20+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min},$ *dye* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(10\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(10\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{10Q}{5(20+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{20+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =9-\frac{2Q}{20+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{20+t}\,Q=9.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(20+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|20+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(20+t)^{2}} \\  & =(20+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(20+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(20+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{20+t}\,Q) & =(20+t)^{2}\cdot 9 \\ (20+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(20+t)Q & =9(20+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(20+t)^{2}) & =9(20+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(20+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 9(20+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(20+t)^{2} & =9\cdot \frac{1}{3}(20+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =3(20+t)+\frac{C}{(20+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $20\,\text{lb}$ of dye. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=20,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =20 \\ 3(20+0)+\frac{C}{(20+0)^{2}} & =20 \\ 60+\frac{C}{(20)^{2}} & =20 \\ \frac{C}{(20)^{2}} & =-40 \\ C & =-40(20)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =3(20+t)-\frac{40(20)^{2}}{(20+t)^{2}} \\  & =3(20+t)-40{(\frac{20}{20+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $180\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=180$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =180 \\ 100+15{t}_{o}-10{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 100+5{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 5{t}_{o} & =80 \\ {t}_{o} & =16\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of dye in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(16) & =3(20+16)-40{(\frac{20}{20+16})}^{2} \\  & =108-40{(\frac{20}{36})}^{2} \\  & ≈95.7\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A wastewater treatment tank at a chemical plant can hold up to $180\,\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $120\,\text{gal}$ of wastewater with $40\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved contaminant. A more concentrated wastewater stream with concentration $1.25\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $8\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which contaminant enters the tank minus the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank.

$$

$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant enters the tank.

First, note that a solution containing $1.25\,\text{lb/gal}$ of contaminant enters the tank at a rate of $12\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminant* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(1.25\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(1.25\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =15\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant exits the tank.

To find the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $120\,\text{gal}$ of liquid; solution enters at $12\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $8\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=120+12t-8t=4(30+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $8\,\text{gal/min},$ *contaminant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(8\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(8\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{8Q}{4(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{30+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =15-\frac{2Q}{30+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q=15.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(30+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|30+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(30+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(30+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q) & =(30+t)^{2}\cdot 15 \\ (30+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(30+t)Q & =15(30+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2}) & =15(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 15(30+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(30+t)^{2} & =15\cdot \frac{1}{3}(30+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =5(30+t)+\frac{C}{(30+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $40\,\text{lb}$ of contaminant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=40,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =40 \\ 5(30+0)+\frac{C}{(30+0)^{2}} & =40 \\ 150+\frac{C}{(30)^{2}} & =40 \\ \frac{C}{{30}^{2}} & =-110 \\ C & =-110(30)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =5(30+t)-\frac{110(30)^{2}}{(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =5(30+t)-110{(\frac{30}{30+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $180\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=180$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =180 \\ 120+12{t}_{o}-8{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 120+4{t}_{o} & =180 \\ 4{t}_{o} & =60 \\ {t}_{o} & =15\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(15) & =5(30+15)-110{(\frac{30}{30+15})}^{2} \\  & =225-110{(\frac{30}{45})}^{2} \\  & ≈176.1\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A processing tank initially holds $420\,\text{L}$ of liquid containing $10\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved preservative.
A feed solution containing $0.05\,\text{kg/L}$ of the preservative is pumped into the tank at a rate of $18\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of $12\,\text{L/min}.$
Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of preservative in the tank $15$ minutes after pumping begins.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $Q$ be the amount of preservative in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which preservative enters the tank minus the rate at which preservative leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which preservative enters the tank.

Note that a feed solution containing $0.05\,\text{kg/L}$ of the preservative enters the tank at a rate of $18\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *preservative* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.05\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (18\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0.9\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which preservative exits the tank.

To find the rate at which preservative leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $420\,\text{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at $18\,\text{L/min}$ and leaves at $12\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the volume of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
420+18t-12t=(420+6t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of preservative in the tank, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{420+6t}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $12\,\text{L/min},$ *preservative* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(12\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{420+6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{420+6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{12Q}{420+6t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{70+t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.9-\frac{2Q}{70+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{70+t}Q=0.9.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(70+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|70+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(70+t)^{2}} \\  & =(70+t)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(70+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(70+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{70+t}Q) & =(70+t)^{2}\cdot 0.9 \\ (70+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(70+t)Q & =0.9(70+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(70+t)^{2}) & =0.9(70+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(70+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 0.9(70+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(70+t)^{2} & =0.9\cdot \frac{1}{3}(70+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =0.3(70+t)+\frac{C}{(70+t)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $10\,\text{kg}$ of preservative. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=10,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =10 \\ 0.3(70+0)+\frac{C}{(70+0)^{2}} & =10 \\ 21+\frac{C}{{70}^{2}} & =10 \\ \frac{C}{{70}^{2}} & =-11 \\ C & =-11(70)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.3(70+t)-\frac{11(70)^{2}}{(70+t)^{2}} \\  & =0.3(70+t)-11{(\frac{70}{70+t})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,  the amount of preservative in the tank $15$ minutes after pumping begins is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(15) & =0.3(70+15)-11{(\frac{70}{70+15})}^{2} \\  & =25.5-11{(\frac{70}{85})}^{2} \\  & ≈18.04\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A fermentation tank initially holds $180\,\text{L}$ of liquid containing $5\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved nutrient.
A solution containing $0.04\,\text{kg/L}$ of dissolved nutrient is pumped into the tank at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid is drained out at a rate of $30\,\text{L/min}.$ If the amount of nutrient $Q(t),$ in kilograms, in the tank $t$ minutes after pumping begins is given by

$$
Q(t)=\alpha \,(1-\frac{t}{18})+\beta {(1-\frac{t}{18})}^{3}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants, what is the value of $\alpha -\beta ?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which minerals enter the tank minus the rate at which minerals leave the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which minerals enter the tank.

First, note that a water solution containing $0.04\,\text{kg/L}$ of minerals enters the tank at a rate of $20\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *minerals* enter the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.04\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (20\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.04\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (20\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0.8\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which minerals exit the tank.

To find the rate at which minerals leave the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $180\,\text{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at $20\,\text{L/min}$ and leaves at $30\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the amount of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
180+20t-30t=(180-10t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of minerals in the tank, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{180-10t}\,\text{kg/L}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $30\,\text{L/min},$ *minerals* leave at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(30\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{180-10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(30\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{180-10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{30Q}{180-10t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{3Q}{18-t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0.8-\frac{3Q}{18-t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{18-t}Q=0.8.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 3/(18-t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{-3\operatorname{ln}⁡|18-t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(18-t)^{-3}} \\  & =(18-t)^{-3}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(18-t)^{-3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(18-t)^{-3}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{3}{18-t}Q) & =(18-t)^{-3}\cdot 0.8 \\ (18-t)^{-3}\frac{dQ}{dt}+3(18-t)^{-4}Q & =0.8(18-t)^{-3} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(18-t)^{-3}) & =0.8(18-t)^{-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(18-t)^{-3})\,dt & =\int 0.8(18-t)^{-3}\,dt \\ Q(18-t)^{-3} & =0.8\cdot \frac{1}{2}(18-t)^{-2}+C \\ Q(t) & =0.4(18-t)+C(18-t)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $C$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $5\,\text{kg}$ of minerals. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=5,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =5 \\ C(18-0)^{3}+0.4(18-0) & =5 \\ C(18)^{3}+7.2 & =5 \\ C & =-\frac{2.2}{{18}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.4(18-t)-\frac{2.2}{{18}^{3}}(18-t)^{3} \\  & =0.4\cdot 18\,(\frac{18-t}{18})-2.2{(\frac{18-t}{18})}^{3} \\  & =7.2\,(1-\frac{t}{18})-2.2{(1-\frac{t}{18})}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have $\alpha =7.2,\beta =-2.2,$ and

$$
\alpha -\beta =7.2-(-2.2)=9.4.
$$
